title: I Let the Community-Radio Booth Clock Catch the Host Who Camped My Mic

parts.text: I stepped into booth B at 6:02 p.m. and host Ellis was already using labeled dynamic mic. The board said: ONE HOUR. LIVE BOARD. MICS STAY WITH THE SLOT. I was twenty-nine, volunteer producer, holding a playlist that listed our hour. Ellis shrugged. "Hosts are the station." I photographed the board, the log, and his voice on my channel. Then I asked for the booth clock. At 6:09 the master control pinged why Ellis was still hot on my fader. I kept my voice indoor and let the timestamp talk. A paper policy is only paper until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: Master control can hear Ellis on my channel during our hour.

social.video_title: He camped my labeled mic in booth B — Part 1/2
social.description: Community radio, a host on my fader, a one-hour clock he posted. I logged the channel. Would you have asked for the booth clock?

parts.text: Ellis called it levels until the desk asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the board, and the fader still. The mic went back to my labeled stand. Ellis ran a slot of their own and told the next host atmosphere was always about optics. Optics is a word people use when a booking exists. Policy now has a second line: HOSTS ARE NOT THE STATION. I keep our hour on a labeled cart. Ellis brown-bags his levels. The booth finally looks like a slot, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.video_title: Hosts are not the station — Part 2/2
social.description: Booth clock, labeled mic, and a second line on the board. Were levels ever my hour?
